headline.main: Interview with Pelicot Daughter Caroline Darian: "My Father No Longer Exists for Me"
headline.social: Interview with Pelicot Daughter Caroline Darian: "My Father No Longer Exists for Me"

intro: Her father is a serial rapist and her mother was his victim. Caroline Darian is the daughter of Gisèle and Dominique Pelicot. Here, she talks about how the case tormented the family and her own certainty that she, too, was abused by her father.
text:
Caroline Darian, 46, is the daughter of Gisèle and Dominique Pelicot. Over the course of almost an entire decade, her mother was secretly drugged by her father – and he then filmed her as she was raped by him and more than 80 other men. It was the highest profile criminal case of the last year.
Darian followed the trial in Avignon for almost four months. In contrast to her mother, who consistently curbed her fury about what had happened, Darian screamed in court, berated her father and left the courtroom in tears when she could no longer take it. In the case of Gisèle, the evidence was overwhelming, thanks to the extensive video material. Caroline Darian, though, will have to live in doubt as to whether her father sexually abused her as well.
Darian has now written a book about the case (Caroline Darian, "I’ll Never Call Him Dad Again”). She says it has helped her deal with the horror. And with the weight of being both the rapist’s daughter and a victim. This conversation took place in the offices of her Paris publishing company.
DER SPIEGEL: Madame Darian, four weeks have now passed since the verdict was announced in Avignon. What were your experiences of December 19, the day when your father was sentenced to 20 years in prison?
Darian: It was a special day for me. In part because I knew it would be the last time I would see the man who fathered me. It wasn’t clear to me in advance just how fast everything would go. The verdict was announced extremely quickly. I wasn’t prepared for that.
DER SPIEGEL: Do you believe the verdicts were just?
Darian: My father earned the most severe punishment. That, at least, is just. Yet he and his lawyer will do all they can to secure his release from prison before the 20 years have elapsed because he is already 72. For me, that is an unbearable thought. I want him to spend the rest of his life in prison.
DER SPIEGEL: Because he has earned it or because you want to be safe from him?
Darian: I don’t believe that perversion can be cured. He will always be a danger, always. Unless he is drugged for the rest of his life.
DER SPIEGEL: The sentences for the 50 co-defendants are between four and 15 years. Prosecutors had demanded far more. You seemed disappointed when those verdicts were announced.
Darian: I was, to be honest. More than half of the defendants were sentenced to less than 10 years. In France, the average sentence for rape without aggravating circumstances is 11 years. The men got off easy for what they did. And if one of the considerations when handing down the verdicts was preventing appeals, it was unsuccessful. Seventeen of them are challenging the verdict. A bunch of men who still don’t get it. And who only want to save their skins.
DER SPIEGEL: Do you really believe that you will never again see the man you no longer refer to as your father?
Darian: I only call him Dominique. If I ever see him again, it will be for another trial involving our family.
DER SPIEGEL: You are determined to never visit him in prison?
Darian: I have asked myself that very question and considered whether I would receive answers to the open questions I still have. But I am convinced that even in prison, I wouldn’t learn the truth.
DER SPIEGEL: In the data on your father’s computer, police found two half-naked photos of you sleeping. The images show you in positions in which, as you have said, you never sleep. And dressed in underwear that doesn’t belong to you. You are therefore convinced that your father sedated you as well?
Darian: There is, for me, no question about it. I sleep lightly. I would have woken up if someone had changed my clothes and repositioned me on the bed. For 20 years, I have been living with a man who works for a morning show on television and who has to get up extremely early. Even still, I wake up every time.
DER SPIEGEL: Had you hoped to learn more about those photos during the trial?
Darian: Of course. I held onto that hope until the very last day. One of the photos was taken in my home near Paris, the room is very clearly recognizable. But when was it exactly? And what exactly did he do to me? During the investigation, Dominique provided five or six different explanations for the photos. In court, he denied ever having taken them. But if not him, who else would it have been? Who was in my house? What happened?
DER SPIEGEL: You believe that you were also abused?
Darian: Yes, because nothing else makes any sense. Why would he sedate me and then stop? That makes no sense. This man has no filter, he knows no limits. Look at what he did to my mother. I have no doubt that I was raped as well. There is nothing random about the photos. In both of them, I am lying in precisely the same position, on my left side, just like my mother in the videos. But in contrast to her, I am like most victims of rape: I have no proof.
DER SPIEGEL: If he did rape you, why wouldn’t he admit it?
Darian: Because it is impossible for him to admit that he committed incest. It would destroy the image he has created of himself. That is why he insists that he never touched his children or his grandchildren. He is lying. My mother also doesn’t know the whole truth. She still doesn’t know when the first rape took place. Or how many men actually raped her. It was far more than the 50 who were in court.
DER SPIEGEL: Are there other indications that your father may have abused you?
Darian: In 2019, I had to undergo several operations for gynecological problems. At the time, I couldn’t understand how they might have developed. Today, I wonder if there might be a connection to the photos.
DER SPIEGEL: In court, it sometimes seemed as though your father still hoped that the family could forgive him for what he did.
Darian: Yes, he tried to reestablish a connection with all of us, especially to my mother. Sometimes, it seemed to me as if he wanted to draw an invisible line to my mother from the glass box where he was sitting. But I won’t allow myself to be manipulated any longer. I only see him as that which he is: a criminal, a serial rapist.
DER SPIEGEL: In contrast to your mother, you castigated your father in the courtroom, rebuked him, shouted out all of your rage and questioned him aggressively. Did you make a conscious decision not to play the quiet victim?
Darian: I don’t think there are good and bad victims. I am completely different than my mother. I needed it, this quest for the truth. Plus, there is a decisive difference: My mother basically knows what happened to her. I don’t. Yet I still have to rebuild my life. Behind me lie four years that were like a tsunami. Of course there is hatred. And the feeling of having been the victim of an enormous injustice.
DER SPIEGEL: Because you don’t feel as though you’ve been taken seriously as a victim?
Darian: There was no real place for me in the courtroom. For me, it was never just about the fact that he photographed me. I was sedated by him, I’m sure of it. Why did nobody ever think to take a hair sample from me?
DER SPIEGEL: During the trial, an increasing distance between you and your mother was clearly apparent. Is that because she has a hard time imagining that you were also a victim of her husband?
Darian: My mother has a different view of the situation. The idea that I was also a victim is certainly a difficult one for her to bear. It is extremely painful for me; I can’t put it any differently. But that’s how it is. Still, I wouldn’t say there is any alienation or distance between us, but a different perception that each of us has.
DER SPIEGEL: In 2023, you founded an association called M’endors pas, "Don’t Drug Me.” The goal of the association is to educate people about "chemical subjugation” – meaning the use of chemicals to sedate and sexually abuse a victim. How far along are you with this work?
Darian: We are currently in talks with the health authorities here regarding the practicality of using a test kit in public hospitals to prove chemical subjugation. Not every laboratory is currently able to do so. In cooperation with the authorities, we also want to train medical personnel and raise their awareness of the issue. It has often been the case that symptoms go unrecognized or are incorrectly interpreted.
DER SPIEGEL: More knowledge is the primary need?
Darian: Definitely. And greater vigilance. If a person you know well starts speaking incoherently and behaving oddly, you should ask yourself some questions and consider whether they may have been drugged.
DER SPIEGEL: Do you feel a sense of guilt for not having seen signs that you perhaps should have picked up?
Darian: I’ve often told myself that if I knew then what I know now, I would have been able to interpret a lot of things better. Her constant blackouts, her hair loss, her rapid weight loss, her extreme sleep disorders. Sometimes, there were entire nights when she couldn’t sleep.
DER SPIEGEL: Were there other symptoms?
Darian: She sometimes sounded like she was drunk on the phone. One time, my son, who was six years old at the time, was talking to her on the phone and said: Grandma is strange somehow. I took the phone and asked her what day it was. She didn’t know.
DER SPIEGEL: The doctors your mother consulted at the time said the symptoms were consistent with early-stage Alzheimer's.
Darian: Nobody came up with a different diagnosis. She also had a number of gynecological problems, which is why I made an appointment for her at my gynecologist. Her cervix was severely inflamed. But nobody voiced suspicions of sexual abuse – which is certainly not an obvious conclusion to draw for a woman of her age. But still, doctors need to be more vigilant.
DER SPIEGEL: Is your involvement in M’endors pas also motivated by a need to set an example against your father?
Darian: I am doing it for myself and for other victims. My father no longer exists for me. He died four years ago – at least the father I thought I knew. Since then, I have discovered the flip side of his personality, and it is horrific. And I believe that we still don’t know everything.
DER SPIEGEL: Please explain.
Darian: There are two cold cases from many years ago that were briefly mentioned in the trial. The investigations are ongoing. Furthermore, he has also been charged with sexually abusing one of his grandchildren.
DER SPIEGEL: One of those cold cases involves an employee at a real estate agency who was drugged, raped and murdered in 1991. The other is an attempted rape from 1999, also in Paris, that has been connected to Dominque Pelicot: An employee of a real estate agency was drugged but was able to escape. Your father’s DNA was found at the scene. He has since confessed to the crime. Your father may have been a sex offender for a long time.
Darian: I have known for four years that I was raised by someone who lied to us and betrayed us. It’s not like he just woke up one morning and was perverted. That’s not a thing. Not if you display the degree of perversity that he has. I am convinced that it had been going on for a long time. And that we will discover a few more cases.
DER SPIEGEL: Despite it all, though, he remains your father. In your book, your tone is almost tender as you describe good, happy times with him. How he would sing Barry White songs in the car on the way to vacation. How he taught your son to swim.
Darian: I now know that everything was built on sand. I can no longer believe him. In my eyes, he betrayed us from A to Z. Did he ever tell the truth? Did he seriously mean it one single time in his life when he told us he loved us? It is impossible for me to continue to look benignly at this past.
DER SPIEGEL: In court, your brother David spoke of the feeling he has that his childhood and youth have been extinguished. Together with him, you destroyed all of the family photo albums, just a few days after you learned of the crimes.
Darian: That was in early November 2020. We were helping our mother clear out the house in Mazan. At some point, I found this box full of photo albums. I told my brothers that it was impossible to keep them. We threw them all into a big pile in the yard and burned them. All of them.
DER SPIEGEL: A radical step. You incinerated your own past. What did your mother say about it?
Darian: She was in a state of distress at the time. She was paralyzed, in shock. Later, she was a little upset at us for destroying everything. But why should we have kept the pictures? I no longer have a single photo of Dominique, and that’s a good thing.
DER SPIEGEL: There is a lot separating you from your mother, but you recently said that you are very proud of her.
Darian: Yes, because she was so courageous to open the doors of this courtroom and to use her fate to set a process in motion, perhaps even to bring about change in society. I was always of the opinion that this trial should not be held behind closed doors. Doing so would have been a gift to all the men. But she was the one who withstood it day after day, who stood up to her rapists. And for that, she has earned our gratitude.
DER SPIEGEL: Were you surprised by her courage, her strength, her dignity?
Darian: No. I don’t know her any differently. Never give up, never show weakness. It would have been unbearable for her to stand there as the humiliated, subjugated victim.
DER SPIEGEL: In your book, you compare her to a medieval queen standing in a field of ruins, head held high, chin raised.
Darian: She always had that side. Laugh together, but never show the tears. Just keep going. We are very different, also because I belong to a different generation. But what she has done is absolutely remarkable.
DER SPIEGEL: Have you been able to recover somewhat since the trial?
Darian: I spent some time at our vacation home on the Atlantic coast with my husband, my son and friends. That was good for me.
DER SPIEGEL: Your father even had your mother raped in that house, by a man he summoned there in 2019. In your bed. There are videos of that rape as well.
Darian: It’s true, he really spared us nothing. And yet, life goes on. With M’endors pas, we have introduced the issue of chemical subjugation into the political debate. That’s not nothing. We have spoken about the issue with two prime ministers, and we are now talking with the third. It is a long journey, but we are making progress.
DER SPIEGEL: Madame Darian, thank you for this interview.
